newsitem.title: USA: Nova Scotia warns against delaying Sable pipe.
newsitem.headline: Nova Scotia warns against delaying Sable pipe.

text.p: Nova Scotia premier John Savage on Tuesday urged Canada regulators to approve a proposed pipeline that would bypass Quebec, saying any delays could hurt the project that aims to supply New England with natural gas.

However, Quebec premier Lucien Bouchard made it clear that he supported a competing plan that would funnel the natural gas through his province, and urged the country's federal government to make the choice strictly according to economics.
The two Canada premiers spoke to reporters at the Annual Conference of the New England Governors and the Eastern Canadian Premiers, which is being held in Newport, Rhode Island.

So far, only one proposal has been submitted to Canada's National Energy Board, which is weighing whether to let a Maritimes & Northeast pipeline be built at a cost of C$1 billion. The line would carry natural gas from the Sable field offshore Nova Scotia to energy-hungry New England states, which rely heavily on imports.
The project, which would not use Canada's present pipeline network, has been put forward by Westcoast Energy Inc, Corp, and Mobil Corp's Mobil Oil Canada unit.

"The key issue that concerns the offshore development project in Nova Scotia is delay," Nova Scotia's Savage said. "We understand from the proponents that there is a window of opportunity in the renegotiation."
"That's our fundamental reason for saying 'make the decision on what is before the Board'," he added later.

The Maritimes & Northeast project is further along than the competing proposal, which also would cost C$1 billion, and which is backed by TransCanada Pipelines Ltd, in partnership with Gaz Metropolitain & Co LP.

In late May, the Maritimes & Northeast proposal to ship 178 million cubic feet of gas per day to New England was deemed "environmentally acceptable" by the U.S. Federal Regulatory Commission. Final approval from Washington was expected at the end of August.
However, Quebec's Bouchard showed no signs of backing off from his support for building a pipeline that would run through his province, and make use of the existing lines in Canada.

"It's not political, nothing to do with any political elements, just what is the best economic project, which is the project that makes the best economic sense, which will produce the best benefit for the people," Bouchard said.

Bouchard also held out the possibility that Canada's federal regulators might opt to approve parts of each project, though he did not elaborate. "I think it will be for the federal government to make a very important decision," he said.
